title: A good opponent
hookLine: difficulties show who we are, like a trainer pairing you with a rough young wrestler (Discourses 1.24)
carry: what is this making of me

cards: In a boxing gym, the coach looks over the new kid and pairs him, on purpose, not with the easiest partner but with someone a little rougher, a little stronger, someone who makes him sweat and sometimes puts him down.
He goes home sore and annoyed. A few months on, he moves differently. Epictetus took that gym wisdom and pointed it at the hardest things in life.

teach.b: This is Discourses book one, chapter twenty-four, on how to struggle with circumstances. It opens with a short line: it's difficulties that show what people are. Then the picture.
When a difficulty lands on you, Epictetus says, remember that God, like a wrestling trainer, has paired you with a rough young opponent. Why?
So that you can become an Olympic champion, and that doesn't happen without sweat. Then something bold.
No one, he tells his student, has ever been handed a better difficulty than yours, if you're willing to use it the way an athlete uses a tough sparring partner. Notice what he's not saying.
Not that the difficulty is good in itself, or that you deserved it, or that suffering is secretly pleasant. The opponent is rough. It hurts.
What he changes is the question.

teach.h: WHAT IS THIS MAKING OF ME?
teach.b: Instead of, why is this happening to me, he asks: what is this making of me? A sparring partner isn't your enemy, even when he puts you on the mat.
He's how you find out what you've got, and how you get more of it. For the Stoics, the trainer is God, the reason that runs the world. Some readers keep that, and some keep only the gym.
Either way, a hard conversation, a setback at work, a stubborn habit can be read as the partner your training needed.

how: Some Stoic practitioners reframe a difficulty as a training partner, asking what virtue it calls on, a habit drawn from this chapter's wrestling image.

o: an enemy you have to beat before you can rest
a friend who always takes your side in a fight
a hardship that trains you, like a rough gym partner

s: Epictetus says difficulty is pleasant if you think about it right
the opponent is rough and it hurts; he changes the question, not the pain.
chapter 1.24 opens by saying difficulties show what people are
not comfortable days, but hard ones.
in his image, God is like a wrestling trainer
who pairs you with a rough young opponent so you can become a champion.

games.q: a hard thing has landed on you. you're Epictetus' student. what does he say to remember?
o: the trainer has paired you with a rough opponent, so you can grow.
avoid it until it goes away.
games.why: he says God, like a wrestling trainer, has matched you with a rough young man, and no one has had a more useful difficulty, if you use it.

practice: Bring to mind one difficulty you're facing now, and picture it not as a wall but as a rough young opponent across the mat. What is it working in you: patience, courage, honesty, endurance?
Step onto the mat in your mind, not happy about it, just willing; you don't have to win today.

wordCard.voice: Sparring partner. Epictetus' name for hardship: the rough partner a trainer chooses for you, so you find out what you've got, and grow it.

orig.note: Greek antagōnistēs: opponent, rival in a contest (our word antagonist); the wrestling partner in Epictetus' image.

carryVoice: Your line: what is this making of me. The opponent is rough, and the training is real. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Discourses 1.24 (how we should struggle with circumstances)
